title: Camp 2 close: the porch
hook: seventy-five stories from a dozen homes; next, the practices

segments.voice: Yesterday, why every story gets its source. Your line was a teaching with no address can't be visited.
screen: `A TEACHING WITH NO ADDRESS CAN'T BE VISITED.`

segments.voice: An old porch at the end of a long summer day. The light is going gold. Someone in a creaky chair says, did I ever tell you about, and everyone settles in, because a story is coming. For seventy-five days, that's where you've been sitting. Early in camp two there was a real porch, too: the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught in the open, which gave the Stoics their name. Today the camp of stories closes: a look back, then a step inside.
screen: `A PORCH AT GOLDEN HOUR.` → `DID I EVER TELL YOU ABOUT…` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: Look who came. The Stoics first: Marcus arguing with himself under the blankets, Epictetus and his master's leg, Zeno's shipwreck, Cleanthes hauling water at night. Cato's last night, Seneca counting his hours, Diogenes asking Alexander to step out of his sunlight. Nasruddin, searching for his key under the lamp and feeding soup to his coat. The Zen teachers, pouring tea until it spilled, and saying is that so. The Taoists: Zhuangzi's butterfly, Cook Ding's knife, the old man's horse. The Jewish sages: Hillel on one foot, Honi's carob tree, Zusya being Zusya. Aesop's tortoise, and his reeds. Rabia's torch, Rumi's elephant, the desert monks' leaking basket and their fingers of flame. The Buddha's mustard seed, arrow and raft. Mencius at the well, Confucius at the river, Satyakama's truth, Guru Nanak's honest bread. A Samaritan and a running father. Socrates asking questions to the end, Brother Lawrence at the sink, Julian's hazelnut, Francis and the wolf, Pascal's coat, Thoreau's cabin. A dozen homes, each named, each left in its own house. Here's what stories can do that ideas can't: they come when called. Blamed unfairly, and Hakuin may show up. Grieving, and Kisa Gotami may walk beside you down the street. About to judge, and you might hear sand running out behind you. You don't have to memorize them. They walk with you now. Camp three is the practices: breath, a morning preview and an evening review, gratitude, walking, service, a sunset ritual, simple things you do with your body and your day. The stories showed what's possible. The practices are how people have walked toward it.
screen: `STOICS, CYNICS AND NASRUDDIN.` · `ZEN, TAO, THE SAGES, AESOP.` · `SUFIS, MONKS, MANY HOUSES, SAINTS.` · `NEXT: THE PRACTICES.` · then, large: `THEY WALK WITH YOU NOW.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit where you did day one, the chair, the step, the corner of the bed; if you can't, picture it. Notice what's the same, the light, the sounds, your body in this seat, and what's different: a whole camp of stories carried here since then. Let one of them come to mind, whichever arrives first, and welcome it like an old friend on the porch.
Porch. Where seventy-five days of stories from a dozen homes were heard, like Zeno's painted porch that gave the Stoics their name.
Your line: they walk with you now. When something hard comes, one may show up. That's camp two.

howItsDone: Across traditions, stories are how wisdom is carried day to day: Christians recall parables, Buddhists Jataka tales and similes, Sikhs the Janamsakhis, Jews the tales of the sages, and philosophers the lives of the Stoics.

fork.reveal: Hakuin, wrongly blamed, said only is that so, and cared for the child in front of him. that's how stories walk with you: they come when called.
